newsitem.title: INDIA: Lehman official urges India to speed disinvestment.
newsitem.headline: Lehman official urges India to speed disinvestment.

text.p: India must speed up the deregulation of its economy and use the proceeds from sales of stakes in public firms to retire its massive debt burden, Lehman Brothers vice-chairman Howard Clark said on Wednesday.

"Lehman's experience with privatisation and disinvestment in other emerging economies has convinced me that disinvesment is a powerful prescription for improving the economy and creating a positive environment for private sector business," Clark said.

Clark, leading a delegation of U.S. businessmen to India to meet officials of the federal government that took power in June, said the relatively slow pace of disinvestment was preventing increased foreign investment flows.
The United States, which invested an estimated $192.4 million in India in 1995/96 (April/March) according to India's central bank, is the largest foreign investor in India.

Indian Prime Minister H.D. Deve Gowda recently set the country a target of attracting $10 billion of foreign direct investment each year. The bulk of this is needed to shore up the crumbling infrastructure sector, crucial to the success of a reform programme started in 1991.
"Debt service absorbs over 40 percent of every dollar," Clark said. "This makes it hard for India to fund the education, social services and infrastructure needed to facilitate rapid development."

Many of India's state-owned enterprises are inefficient and overstaffed, and a drain on state finances, Clark said. Even enterprises in the black yield only a fraction of the potential return on investment, compared with private sector firms in the same sectors.
"The solution is clear. The government must sell off these companies and use the proceeds to retire debt," Clark said.
India plans to raise 50 billion rupees in 1996/97 (April-March) through the sale of partial stakes in state-owned units.

Another member of the delegation, Tommy Thompson, vice-president of Texas-based Coastal Power Co, said it would be easy for India to generate its entire $10 billion foreign direct investment target from American firms alone.
"American companies are ready and willing and eager to bring these investments into India and meet the target," he said.
But delegation members said the country would have to allay some of the foreign investors' fears.
"India must make it clear that foreign investment is welcome without restrictions and limitations," said Richard Johannessen, president of Ingersoll-Rand Asia Pacific.
"It must have a meaningful intellectual property rights law to attract more foreign investment."

U.S. firms seeking to invest in India's infrastructure sector want to put their money in housing rather than ports, roads, power or telecommunications sectors where the Indian government would prefer direct investment, delegates said.
David Wolf, president of the Fremont Group, said he believed U.S. firms would invest $1 billion in India annually if the laws were changed to allow them to venture into the housing sector.

"There is a tremendous shortage of good quality housing," Wolf said. "The firms could bring in low-cost modern techniques to build homes that are energy-efficient and material-efficient. Lots of ancillary companies could be set up here."
